idiom_name: POSIX message queue (mq_open/mq_send/mq_receive) or hand-rolled ring buffer + pthread mutex/condvar
implementation_notes: The channel must be hand-written: the nearest operating-system primitive is the POSIX message queue, where mq_send appends and mq_receive removes exactly one message (the oldest of the highest priority) and is documented MT-Safe, so several worker threads or processes can share it without coordinating with each other. Because mq_receive demands a buffer as large as the queue's mq_msgsize attribute, many programs instead build a bounded ring buffer behind a pthread_mutex and pthread_cond_t and hand each item to one waiter - the POSIX queue when the peers are separate processes and payloads are small, the ring buffer when payloads vary or an existing threading model must be reused.
pitfalls: mq_receive fails with EMSGSIZE when the caller's buffer is smaller than mq_msgsize; it never truncates, so message sizing is a hard contract.
POSIX message queues are priority-ordered (highest priority first), not FIFO, unless every message is sent at the same priority.
Queue objects are named kernel resources: they survive the process, so they must be mq_close'd and mq_unlink'd or the next start fails with EEXIST.
A full queue plus a blocking mq_send deadlocks a single-threaded reader; bound producers or use O_NONBLOCK with a retry policy.
